label: Bacteriology
blurb: Gram stain, catalase, coagulase, hemolysis, lactose — and the diseases they cause

organisms.name: Staphylococcus aureus
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters, catalase positive, coagulase positive, beta-hemolytic, ferments mannitol (yellow on mannitol salt agar), golden pigment
organisms.manifestations: Skin and soft tissue abscess, acute endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, pneumonia after influenza, toxic shock syndrome, scalded skin syndrome, rapid-onset food poisoning
organisms.treatment: Nafcillin or oxacillin for MSSA; vancomycin for MRSA; add clindamycin for toxin suppression in toxic shock
organisms.transmission: Direct contact and nasal carriage; preformed toxin in mayonnaise, custard, and meats for food poisoning
organisms.virulenceFactor: Protein A binds IgG Fc to block opsonization; TSST-1 superantigen cross-links MHC II and TCR; exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1
organisms.tooltip: Coagulase positive separates it from all other staph. Protein A is the classic virulence factor. Causes both rapid-onset food poisoning from preformed toxin and post-influenza pneumonia.

organisms.name: Staphylococcus epidermidis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, forms biofilm, common blood culture contaminant
organisms.manifestations: Prosthetic valve endocarditis, prosthetic joint infection, central line-associated bloodstream infection, CSF shunt infection
organisms.treatment: Vancomycin, because most isolates are methicillin resistant; device removal is usually required
organisms.transmission: Normal skin flora introduced during device placement or venipuncture
organisms.virulenceFactor: Polysaccharide capsule and biofilm (slime layer) that adheres to plastic and shields from antibiotics and phagocytes
organisms.tooltip: Coagulase negative and novobiocin sensitive. Infects anything artificial. A single positive blood culture is usually contamination; multiple positives with a device suggest real infection.

organisms.name: Staphylococcus saprophyticus
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant, urease positive
organisms.manifestations: Uncomplicated cystitis in sexually active young women — the second most common cause after E. coli
organisms.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or nitrofurantoin
organisms.transmission: Normal vaginal and periurethral flora ascending into the bladder
organisms.virulenceFactor: Urease and adhesins that bind uroepithelium
organisms.tooltip: Novobiocin resistant distinguishes it from S. epidermidis: Saprophyticus is Resistant, Epidermidis is Sensitive — 'NO StRES.' Second most common cause of cystitis in young women.

organisms.name: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A)
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive, Lancefield group A
organisms.manifestations: Pharyngitis, impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, scarlet fever, toxic shock-like syndrome; sequelae of rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
organisms.treatment: Penicillin or amoxicillin; add clindamycin for necrotizing fasciitis or toxic shock to suppress toxin production
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets for pharyngitis; direct skin contact for impetigo and cellulitis
organisms.virulenceFactor: M protein inhibits complement and mediates rheumatic fever through molecular mimicry; streptolysin O is antigenic (ASO titer); exotoxin A is a superantigen
organisms.tooltip: Bacitracin sensitive versus group B resistant. M protein drives both immune evasion and rheumatic fever via mimicry of cardiac myosin. Pharyngitis causes both rheumatic fever and PSGN; skin infection causes only PSGN.

organisms.name: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B)
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant, hippurate positive, CAMP test positive, Lancefield group B
organisms.manifestations: Neonatal meningitis, pneumonia, and sepsis; chorioamnionitis and postpartum endometritis; soft tissue infection in diabetics
organisms.treatment: Penicillin or ampicillin; intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis for colonized mothers
organisms.transmission: Vertical transmission from maternal vaginal and rectal colonization during delivery
organisms.virulenceFactor: Polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis, and beta-hemolysin
organisms.tooltip: Screen all pregnant women at 35 to 37 weeks and give intrapartum penicillin if positive. Group B is Bacitracin resistant and a cause of Babies' meningitis. CAMP factor and hippurate hydrolysis identify it.

organisms.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci, catalase negative, alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble, encapsulated, quellung reaction positive
organisms.manifestations: Lobar pneumonia (most common cause), adult meningitis (most common cause), otitis media in children, sinusitis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
organisms.treatment: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin for meningitis; amoxicillin or ceftriaxone plus a macrolide for pneumonia
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets; often follows viral upper respiratory infection, with nasopharyngeal colonization preceding disease
organisms.virulenceFactor: Polysaccharide capsule is the key factor; IgA protease aids mucosal invasion; pneumolysin lyses host cells
organisms.tooltip: MOPS: Meningitis, Otitis media, Pneumonia, Sinusitis. Optochin sensitive and bile soluble separate it from viridans. Asplenic and sickle cell patients are at extreme risk from the capsule.

organisms.name: Viridans streptococci
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant, bile insoluble, synthesizes dextrans
organisms.manifestations: Subacute bacterial endocarditis on previously damaged valves, dental caries (S. mutans), brain abscess
organisms.treatment: Penicillin plus gentamicin for endocarditis; amoxicillin prophylaxis before dental procedures in high-risk patients
organisms.transmission: Normal oropharyngeal flora entering the blood during dental procedures or poor oral hygiene
organisms.virulenceFactor: Dextrans that mediate adherence to fibrin-platelet aggregates on damaged valves and to tooth enamel
organisms.tooltip: Optochin resistant and bile insoluble, the mirror image of pneumococcus. Dextran synthesis explains why it sticks to damaged valves — the classic subacute endocarditis after a dental visit.

organisms.name: Enterococcus faecalis / faecium
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains, catalase negative, gamma-hemolytic (variable), grows in 6.5% NaCl and bile, PYR positive, Lancefield group D
organisms.manifestations: Urinary tract infection, biliary tract infection, subacute endocarditis after GI or GU instrumentation, intra-abdominal infection
organisms.treatment: Ampicillin plus gentamicin for faecalis; linezolid or daptomycin for vancomycin-resistant faecium
organisms.transmission: Endogenous colonic flora; nosocomial spread between patients in hospitals
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intrinsic antibiotic resistance and bile and salt tolerance; VanA alters the peptidoglycan terminus from D-ala-D-ala to D-ala-D-lac
organisms.tooltip: Growth in 6.5% NaCl is the identifying feature. VRE resistance comes from swapping D-ala-D-ala for D-ala-D-lac so vancomycin cannot bind. Think endocarditis after colonoscopy.

organisms.name: Clostridioides difficile
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive spore-forming anaerobic rod; diagnosed by stool PCR for toxin genes or toxin EIA; pseudomembranes on colonoscopy
organisms.manifestations: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, colonic perforation
organisms.treatment: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin; fecal microbiota transplant for recurrent disease; stop the inciting antibiotic
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral spread of alcohol-resistant spores in healthcare settings; requires soap and water, not alcohol gel
organisms.virulenceFactor: Toxin A (enterotoxin) damages mucosa and Toxin B (cytotoxin) depolymerizes actin, causing cytoskeletal disruption and cell death
organisms.tooltip: Spores resist alcohol hand gel, so wash with soap and water. Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and broad-spectrum beta-lactams are the usual culprits. Toxin B is the cytotoxin that kills enterocytes.

organisms.name: Clostridium tetani
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive spore-forming obligate anaerobe with terminal spores giving a tennis-racket appearance; diagnosis is clinical
organisms.manifestations: Trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, muscle spasms, autonomic instability; neonatal tetanus from umbilical stump contamination
organisms.treatment: Tetanus immune globulin, metronidazole, wound debridement, benzodiazepines for spasm, and vaccination
organisms.transmission: Spores in soil entering puncture wounds, especially rusty nails and deep contaminated wounds
organisms.virulenceFactor: Tetanospasmin, a protease that cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA from Renshaw cells
organisms.tooltip: Blocks inhibitory neurotransmission, so muscles cannot relax — the opposite of botulism, which blocks excitatory acetylcholine release. Both cleave SNARE proteins.

organisms.name: Clostridium botulinum
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive spore-forming obligate anaerobe; toxin detected in serum, stool, or the suspect food
organisms.manifestations: Descending flaccid paralysis with diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, and bilateral cranial neuropathies; floppy baby syndrome in infants
organisms.treatment: Antitoxin (heptavalent in adults, BabyBIG in infants) and respiratory support; antibiotics are not used in infants
organisms.transmission: Preformed toxin in improperly canned foods in adults; ingested spores in honey for infants under one year
organisms.virulenceFactor: Botulinum toxin, a protease cleaving SNARE proteins to block presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
organisms.tooltip: Adults get preformed toxin from home-canned food; infants get spores from honey that then germinate in the gut. Symmetric descending paralysis with preserved sensation and normal mentation.

organisms.name: Clostridium perfringens
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive spore-forming anaerobic rod, double zone of hemolysis on blood agar, stormy fermentation in milk medium, gas in tissue on imaging
organisms.manifestations: Gas gangrene (myonecrosis) with crepitus, late-onset watery food poisoning 10 to 12 hours after eating, necrotizing enteritis
organisms.treatment: Surgical debridement plus penicillin and clindamycin; hyperbaric oxygen as adjunct for gas gangrene
organisms.transmission: Soil contamination of traumatic or surgical wounds; reheated meats and gravy for food poisoning
organisms.virulenceFactor: Alpha toxin, a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that degrades cell membranes causing myonecrosis and hemolysis
organisms.tooltip: Alpha toxin is a lecithinase producing the double zone of hemolysis and gas in tissue. Its food poisoning has a longer incubation than S. aureus and resolves within 24 hours.

organisms.name: Bacillus anthracis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive spore-forming rod in long chains (medusa head colonies), the only bacterium with a polypeptide capsule of poly-D-glutamate, non-hemolytic
organisms.manifestations: Cutaneous anthrax with a painless black eschar; inhalational anthrax (woolsorter's disease) with mediastinal widening and hemorrhagic mediastinitis; GI anthrax
organisms.treatment: Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline; add antitoxin and multidrug therapy for systemic disease
organisms.transmission: Spores from contaminated animal hides, wool, and soil; inhalation in bioterrorism or industrial exposure
organisms.virulenceFactor: Edema factor is an adenylate cyclase raising cAMP; lethal factor is a protease cleaving MAP kinase; poly-D-glutamate capsule resists phagocytosis
organisms.tooltip: The only bacterium with a protein rather than polysaccharide capsule. Cutaneous lesions are painless black eschars. Inhalational disease shows widened mediastinum on chest x-ray, not pneumonia.

organisms.name: Bacillus cereus
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive spore-forming rod, beta-hemolytic, motile, grows aerobically; diagnosis usually clinical from food history
organisms.manifestations: Emetic syndrome with vomiting 1 to 5 hours after reheated rice; diarrheal syndrome 8 to 18 hours later; keratitis and endophthalmitis after eye trauma
organisms.treatment: Supportive care with fluids for food poisoning; vancomycin or clindamycin for invasive or ocular disease
organisms.transmission: Spores surviving in reheated fried rice, pasta, and other starchy foods left at room temperature
organisms.virulenceFactor: Heat-stable cereulide causing vomiting, and a heat-labile enterotoxin raising cAMP to cause watery diarrhea
organisms.tooltip: The reheated rice organism. Cereulide is preformed and heat stable, so reheating does not help — that is the short-incubation vomiting syndrome.

organisms.name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive club-shaped rods in V and L formations, metachromatic granules on methylene blue, black colonies on tellurite agar, Elek test detects toxin
organisms.manifestations: Pharyngitis with a gray pseudomembrane, bull neck lymphadenopathy, myocarditis with arrhythmia, and peripheral neuropathy
organisms.treatment: Diphtheria antitoxin first, plus penicillin or erythromycin; vaccination with the toxoid prevents it
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and direct contact with lesions from infected or carrier individuals
organisms.virulenceFactor: Diphtheria toxin, encoded by a lysogenic beta-prophage, ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 to halt host protein synthesis
organisms.tooltip: Attempting to scrape the gray pseudomembrane causes bleeding. The toxin is phage-encoded and ADP-ribosylates EF-2 — the same target as Pseudomonas exotoxin A.

organisms.name: Listeria monocytogenes
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive rod with characteristic tumbling motility at 22 to 28 C, cold enrichment (grows at 4 C), weakly beta-hemolytic, catalase positive, facultative intracellular
organisms.manifestations: Meningitis in neonates, elderly, and immunocompromised; granulomatosis infantiseptica; febrile gastroenteritis; spontaneous abortion
organisms.treatment: Ampicillin, often with gentamicin; it is the reason ampicillin is added to empiric meningitis coverage at the age extremes
organisms.transmission: Unpasteurized dairy, soft cheeses, deli meats, and cold smoked fish; transplacental and vaginal transmission at birth
organisms.virulenceFactor: Listeriolysin O escapes the phagosome; actin rockets (ActA) drive cell-to-cell spread while avoiding extracellular antibody
organisms.tooltip: The only gram-positive rod that causes meningitis, and the reason ampicillin is added for neonates, adults over 50, and immunocompromised patients. Actin rockets let it move between cells unseen.

organisms.name: Nocardia asteroides
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive branching filamentous rods, partially acid-fast, aerobe, urease positive, grows slowly on buffered charcoal yeast or Sabouraud media
organisms.manifestations: Cavitary pneumonia in immunocompromised patients, brain abscess, cutaneous infection after soil inoculation
organisms.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, often prolonged; add a carbapenem or amikacin for severe or CNS disease
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of soil dust, or direct inoculation of soil into skin
organisms.virulenceFactor: Catalase and superoxide dismutase resist oxidative killing; mycolic acids in the cell wall confer partial acid-fastness
organisms.tooltip: Nocardia is aerobic, partially acid-fast, and treated with sulfonamides; Actinomyces is anaerobic, not acid-fast, and treated with penicillin. 'SNAP' — Sulfa for Nocardia, Actinomyces Penicillin.

organisms.name: Actinomyces israelii
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-positive branching filamentous rods, not acid-fast, obligate anaerobe, yellow sulfur granules in pus
organisms.manifestations: Cervicofacial abscess with draining sinus tracts through the jaw, pelvic infection associated with IUDs, aspiration pneumonia
organisms.treatment: High-dose penicillin G followed by oral penicillin, often for 6 to 12 months; surgical drainage
organisms.transmission: Normal oral flora invading after dental trauma, surgery, or poor dentition
organisms.virulenceFactor: Ability to form dense filamentous aggregates (sulfur granules) that resist phagocytosis, plus tissue-penetrating sinus tracts
organisms.tooltip: Draining sinus tracts from the jaw after dental work, with yellow sulfur granules in the pus. Anaerobic and not acid-fast, which separates it from Nocardia. Treated with penicillin.

organisms.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
organisms.labFeatures: Acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen stain, aerobic, slow growing on Lowenstein-Jensen medium, niacin and catalase positive, caseating granulomas on histology
organisms.manifestations: Primary infection with Ghon complex; reactivation apical cavitary pneumonia with hemoptysis and night sweats; Pott disease, scrofula, meningitis, and miliary spread
organisms.treatment: Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) for two months, then rifampin and isoniazid for four more
organisms.transmission: Airborne respiratory droplet nuclei from a person with active pulmonary disease; requires airborne isolation
organisms.virulenceFactor: Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) induces TNF release and granuloma formation; sulfatides inhibit phagolysosome fusion
organisms.tooltip: Reactivation prefers the lung apices because oxygen tension is highest there and the organism is an obligate aerobe. Cord factor drives granuloma formation; sulfatides block phagolysosome fusion.

organisms.name: Mycobacterium leprae
organisms.labFeatures: Acid-fast bacillus that cannot be cultured in vitro; grows in armadillos and mouse footpads; prefers cool temperatures
organisms.manifestations: Tuberculoid form with few well-demarcated hypopigmented anesthetic plaques; lepromatous form with diffuse leonine facies, nodules, and glove-and-stocking neuropathy
organisms.treatment: Dapsone plus rifampin for tuberculoid; add clofazimine for lepromatous; treatment lasts months to years
organisms.transmission: Prolonged close contact with respiratory secretions of untreated lepromatous patients; armadillo exposure in the southern United States
organisms.virulenceFactor: Preference for cool superficial tissues (skin, nerves, nose, extremities) and the ability to survive within Schwann cells and macrophages
organisms.tooltip: Tuberculoid is the Th1 response with few organisms and a positive lepromin test; lepromatous is the Th2 response with poor cell-mediated immunity and heavy bacillary load.

organisms.name: Neisseria meningitidis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative kidney-bean diplococci, oxidase positive, maltose and glucose fermenter, grows on Thayer-Martin agar, polysaccharide capsule
organisms.manifestations: Meningitis with petechial or purpuric rash, meningococcemia, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome with adrenal hemorrhage and shock
organisms.treatment: Ceftriaxone; rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone for close-contact prophylaxis; conjugate vaccine for prevention
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and oropharyngeal secretions; outbreaks in dormitories and military barracks
organisms.virulenceFactor: Polysaccharide capsule, IgA protease, lipooligosaccharide endotoxin driving the shock and purpura, and pili for mucosal attachment
organisms.tooltip: Ferments Maltose and Glucose; gonorrhoeae ferments Glucose only. Terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9) causes recurrent Neisseria infection. The vaccine does not cover serogroup B polysaccharide.

organisms.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative diplococci, oxidase positive, ferments glucose only, grows on Thayer-Martin, no polysaccharide capsule, intracellular within neutrophils
organisms.manifestations: Purulent urethritis and cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, septic arthritis in young adults, neonatal conjunctivitis, disseminated infection with pustular rash and tenosynovitis
organisms.treatment: Ceftriaxone, with doxycycline added to cover concurrent chlamydia; erythromycin eye ointment prophylaxis in newborns
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact; vertical transmission during vaginal delivery causing ophthalmia neonatorum
organisms.virulenceFactor: Antigenic variation of pili prevents lasting immunity and blocks vaccine development; IgA protease; opacity proteins
organisms.tooltip: No capsule and no vaccine, because pilus antigenic variation prevents durable immunity — hence reinfection is common. Neonatal conjunctivitis appears days 2 to 5; chlamydial appears days 5 to 14.

organisms.name: Escherichia coli
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose fermenter (pink on MacConkey), indole positive, green metallic sheen on EMB agar, catalase positive, oxidase negative, motile
organisms.manifestations: Most common cause of urinary tract infection; neonatal meningitis; gram-negative sepsis; traveler's diarrhea (ETEC); bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome (EHEC O157:H7)
organisms.treatment: Nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX for cystitis; ceftriaxone for pyelonephritis or sepsis; supportive care only for EHEC, since antibiotics increase HUS risk
organisms.transmission: Ascending fecal flora for UTI; contaminated food and water for diarrheal strains; undercooked ground beef for EHEC
organisms.virulenceFactor: Fimbriae cause cystitis and pyelonephritis; K capsule causes pneumonia and neonatal meningitis; LT and ST toxins cause watery diarrhea; Shiga-like toxin in EHEC inactivates 60S ribosome
organisms.tooltip: EHEC O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol, which is how labs flag it. Never give antibiotics for EHEC — killing the organism releases more Shiga-like toxin and precipitates hemolytic uremic syndrome.

organisms.name: Klebsiella pneumoniae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative encapsulated rod, lactose fermenter, non-motile, urease positive, very large mucoid colonies from the thick capsule
organisms.manifestations: Cavitary lobar pneumonia with thick currant jelly sputum in alcoholics and diabetics, aspiration pneumonia, urinary tract infection, nosocomial sepsis, liver abscess
organisms.treatment: Carbapenem for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers; ceftazidime-avibactam or colistin for carbapenem-resistant strains
organisms.transmission: Aspiration of colonizing oropharyngeal flora; nosocomial spread via healthcare workers and devices
organisms.virulenceFactor: Very large polysaccharide capsule producing the mucoid phenotype and resisting phagocytosis; urease; ESBL and carbapenemase enzymes
organisms.tooltip: The 4 A's: Aspiration pneumonia, Abscess in lungs and liver, Alcoholics, and diAbetics. Currant jelly sputum reflects necrotizing hemorrhagic consolidation from the capsule-driven inflammation.

organisms.name: Proteus mirabilis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose non-fermenter, highly motile with swarming growth on agar, urease positive, fishy odor, alkaline urine
organisms.manifestations: Urinary tract infection with struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) staghorn calculi, chronic pyelonephritis
organisms.treatment: TMP-SMX or a fluoroquinolone, plus complete surgical removal of infected stones
organisms.transmission: Ascending fecal flora into the urinary tract, often in patients with chronic catheters
organisms.virulenceFactor: Urease splits urea into ammonia, raising urine pH to precipitate struvite stones that then harbor bacteria; swarming motility aids ascent
organisms.tooltip: Urease alkalinizes urine, which precipitates struvite staghorn calculi. The stone must come out entirely or infection recurs, since bacteria live inside it. Suspect it with urine pH above 8.

organisms.name: Salmonella Typhi
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose non-fermenter, produces hydrogen sulfide (black colonies on Hektoen), motile with flagella, has Vi capsule, facultative intracellular
organisms.manifestations: Typhoid fever with stepwise rising fever, rose spots on the abdomen, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, pea-soup diarrhea, and intestinal perforation in week 3
organisms.treatment: Ceftriaxone or azithromycin; a fluoroquinolone where susceptible; cholecystectomy may be needed for chronic carriers
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral from contaminated food or water, often from a chronic gallbladder carrier; humans are the only reservoir
organisms.virulenceFactor: Vi polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis; survival within macrophages allows dissemination and gallbladder colonization
organisms.tooltip: Unlike other Salmonella it has a human-only reservoir and colonizes the gallbladder, creating chronic carriers like Typhoid Mary. Antibiotics do help here, unlike nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis.

organisms.name: Salmonella enteritidis (nontyphoidal)
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose non-fermenter, hydrogen sulfide producer, motile, invades the mucosa producing a monocytic infiltrate
organisms.manifestations: Inflammatory diarrhea with fever, sometimes bloody; osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease; bacteremia in the immunocompromised
organisms.treatment: Supportive care only in healthy hosts, since antibiotics prolong the carrier state; treat the very young, elderly, or immunocompromised
organisms.transmission: Undercooked poultry and eggs, unpasteurized milk, and contact with pet reptiles and turtles
organisms.virulenceFactor: Flagella and type III secretion system that injects effectors to force epithelial uptake; endotoxin
organisms.tooltip: Antibiotics prolong fecal shedding in nontyphoidal Salmonella, so withhold them in healthy patients. It is motile and produces H2S, whereas Shigella is non-motile and does not.

organisms.name: Shigella species
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose non-fermenter, non-motile, does not produce hydrogen sulfide, very low infectious dose (as few as 10 organisms)
organisms.manifestations: Bloody mucoid diarrhea with tenesmus and fever (bacillary dysentery), febrile seizures in children, hemolytic uremic syndrome with S. dysenteriae
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin or ceftriaxone for severe disease; fluids; avoid antimotility agents
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral between humans with a very low infectious dose, so person-to-person spread in daycares is common; the four F's — food, fingers, feces, flies
organisms.virulenceFactor: Shiga toxin inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit; invades M cells of Peyer patches and spreads cell to cell via actin polymerization
organisms.tooltip: Non-motile and H2S negative, the mirror of Salmonella. Its extremely low infectious dose explains daycare outbreaks. Shiga toxin also causes HUS, same mechanism as EHEC.

organisms.name: Vibrio cholerae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative comma-shaped rod, oxidase positive, grows in alkaline media (TCBS agar), shooting-star motility, acid labile so a large inoculum is needed
organisms.manifestations: Profuse painless rice-water diarrhea with rapid dehydration, hypovolemic shock, and non-gap metabolic acidosis
organisms.treatment: Aggressive oral or intravenous rehydration is the mainstay; doxycycline or azithromycin shortens shedding
organisms.transmission: Contaminated drinking water and undercooked shellfish, usually in settings with poor sanitation
organisms.virulenceFactor: Cholera toxin permanently activates Gs by ADP-ribosylation, raising cAMP to drive chloride and water secretion through CFTR
organisms.tooltip: Cholera toxin locks Gs on, flooding the lumen with chloride and water. Death is from dehydration, not infection, so rehydration alone saves nearly everyone. Acid labile, so gastric acid is protective.

organisms.name: Campylobacter jejuni
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative comma or S-shaped rod, oxidase positive, grows at 42 C, microaerophilic, darting motility
organisms.manifestations: Bloody inflammatory diarrhea with severe cramping that can mimic appendicitis; antecedent of Guillain-Barre syndrome and reactive arthritis
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; azithromycin or erythromycin if severe or prolonged; avoid fluoroquinolones given resistance
organisms.transmission: Undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk, contaminated water, and contact with infected puppies and other animals
organisms.virulenceFactor: Cytolethal distending toxin; lipooligosaccharide that mimics peripheral nerve gangliosides, triggering autoimmune demyelination
organisms.tooltip: Growth at 42 C is the identifying feature — it is adapted to the avian gut. The most common bacterial antecedent of Guillain-Barre, through ganglioside molecular mimicry.

organisms.name: Helicobacter pylori
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative curved rod, oxidase positive, catalase positive, strongly urease positive (basis of breath and stool tests), microaerophilic
organisms.manifestations: Chronic gastritis, duodenal ulcer (most common cause), gastric ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma, and MALT lymphoma
organisms.treatment: Bismuth quadruple therapy, or clarithromycin-based triple therapy with amoxicillin and a proton pump inhibitor
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral and oral-oral, usually acquired in childhood in crowded conditions
organisms.virulenceFactor: Urease neutralizes gastric acid locally and allows colonization; CagA and VacA injure epithelium and promote carcinogenesis
organisms.tooltip: Urease is both its survival mechanism and the basis of the urea breath test. It is the only bacterium classified as a WHO group 1 carcinogen, causing gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

organisms.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, oxidase positive, lactose non-fermenter, obligate aerobe, blue-green pyocyanin pigment, grape-like odor, biofilm former
organisms.manifestations: Pneumonia in cystic fibrosis and ventilated patients, burn wound sepsis, hot tub folliculitis, otitis externa, malignant otitis in diabetics, ecthyma gangrenosum, corneal ulcer in contact lens wearers
organisms.treatment: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or meropenem, often with an aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone
organisms.transmission: Water reservoirs including sinks, hot tubs, humidifiers, and ventilator tubing; thrives in moist hospital environments
organisms.virulenceFactor: Exotoxin A ADP-ribosylates EF-2 halting protein synthesis; phospholipase C, pyocyanin generating reactive oxygen species, alginate biofilm, and endotoxin
organisms.tooltip: PSEUDOmonas: Pneumonia, Sepsis, Ecthyma gangrenosum, UTI, Diabetic osteomyelitis, Otitis externa. Exotoxin A hits EF-2, the same target as diphtheria toxin. Blue-green pigment with a grape smell.

organisms.name: Haemophilus influenzae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative pleomorphic coccobacillus requiring factors V (NAD) and X (hematin) on chocolate agar; satellite phenomenon around S. aureus; type b has a polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule
organisms.manifestations: Epiglottitis with thumbprint sign and drooling, meningitis in unvaccinated children, otitis media, sinusitis, and COPD exacerbation from nontypeable strains
organisms.treatment: Ceftriaxone for invasive disease; amoxicillin-clavulanate for mucosal infection; rifampin prophylaxis for close contacts
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and direct contact with respiratory secretions
organisms.virulenceFactor: Type b polysaccharide capsule (PRP) resists phagocytosis; IgA protease cleaves mucosal antibody
organisms.tooltip: Needs both factors V and X, hence growth only on chocolate agar. The Hib conjugate vaccine nearly eliminated invasive disease, so epiglottitis now suggests an unvaccinated child.

organisms.name: Legionella pneumophila
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod that stains poorly (use silver stain), requires charcoal yeast extract with iron and cysteine, urine antigen test, facultative intracellular
organisms.manifestations: Severe atypical pneumonia with high fever, relative bradycardia, diarrhea, confusion, and hyponatremia; Pontiac fever as a mild flu-like form
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin or levofloxacin
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of aerosols from contaminated water systems — air conditioning cooling towers, hot tubs, decorative fountains; no person-to-person spread
organisms.virulenceFactor: Survives and replicates within alveolar macrophages by blocking phagolysosome fusion; Dot/Icm type IV secretion system
organisms.tooltip: Pneumonia plus hyponatremia plus diarrhea plus confusion in a smoker — think Legionella and send a urine antigen. Stains poorly on Gram because of its branched-chain fatty acid cell wall.

organisms.name: Bordetella pertussis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative coccobacillus grown on Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium, diagnosed by nasopharyngeal PCR, marked lymphocytosis on CBC
organisms.manifestations: Whooping cough in three stages: catarrhal, paroxysmal with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive emesis, then convalescent; apnea in infants
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin, which limits spread more than it alters the course once paroxysms begin; DTaP and Tdap for prevention
organisms.transmission: Highly contagious respiratory droplets; infants are often infected by an undervaccinated adolescent or adult
organisms.virulenceFactor: Pertussis toxin disables Gi by ADP-ribosylation causing unchecked cAMP rise; filamentous hemagglutinin for attachment; tracheal cytotoxin destroys ciliated cells
organisms.tooltip: Pertussis toxin disables Gi, the opposite of cholera toxin which locks Gs on — both end in excess cAMP. Lymphocytosis rather than neutrophilia is a distinctive clue.

organisms.name: Brucella species
organisms.labFeatures: Small gram-negative coccobacillus, facultative intracellular, slow growing requiring prolonged culture, serology for diagnosis; a laboratory biohazard
organisms.manifestations: Undulant fever with drenching sweats, malaise, arthralgias, hepatosplenomegaly, sacroiliitis, and spinal osteomyelitis
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline plus rifampin, or doxycycline plus streptomycin, for six weeks
organisms.transmission: Unpasteurized dairy from goats, sheep, or cattle; contact with infected animal tissue in farmers, veterinarians, and abattoir workers
organisms.virulenceFactor: Survival within macrophages by inhibiting phagosome-lysosome fusion, allowing chronic reticuloendothelial infection
organisms.tooltip: Undulant fever means it rises and falls over weeks. Unpasteurized goat cheese plus back pain plus sweats is the classic vignette. Requires combination therapy because it hides inside macrophages.

organisms.name: Francisella tularensis
organisms.labFeatures: Small gram-negative coccobacillus requiring cysteine-enriched media, facultative intracellular, highly infectious at very low doses, serology or PCR for diagnosis
organisms.manifestations: Ulceroglandular tularemia with a painful ulcer and regional lymphadenopathy; pneumonic and typhoidal forms; caseating granulomas
organisms.treatment: Streptomycin or gentamicin; doxycycline or ciprofloxacin for milder disease
organisms.transmission: Tick and deerfly bites, handling infected rabbits, and inhalation of aerosols from contaminated soil or lawn mowing
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intracellular survival in macrophages and an exceptionally low infectious dose (as few as 10 organisms), making it a bioterrorism concern
organisms.tooltip: Rabbits and ticks. The infectious dose is so low that laboratory handling requires biosafety level 3. Forms caseating granulomas, so it can mimic tuberculosis histologically.

organisms.name: Yersinia pestis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod with bipolar safety-pin appearance on Wright-Giemsa stain, facultative intracellular, grows at 28 C best
organisms.manifestations: Bubonic plague with painful matted buboes, septicemic plague with purpura and gangrene, and rapidly fatal pneumonic plague
organisms.treatment: Streptomycin or gentamicin; doxycycline or ciprofloxacin as alternatives; strict isolation for pneumonic cases
organisms.transmission: Flea bite from infected rodents, including prairie dogs in the southwestern United States; person-to-person respiratory spread in pneumonic plague
organisms.virulenceFactor: F1 capsular antigen, Yersinia outer proteins (Yops) delivered by type III secretion to disable phagocytes, and plasminogen activator
organisms.tooltip: Safety-pin bipolar staining. Buboes are exquisitely tender, unlike the painless adenopathy of many other infections. Pneumonic plague is the only form that spreads person to person.

organisms.name: Bartonella henselae
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, fastidious and hard to culture, diagnosed serologically; Warthin-Starry silver stain of nodes; bacillary angiomatosis histology
organisms.manifestations: Cat-scratch disease with regional tender lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever; bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis hepatis in HIV; culture-negative endocarditis
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin for cat-scratch disease; doxycycline plus rifampin for bacillary angiomatosis
organisms.transmission: Cat scratch or bite, and cat flea exposure
organisms.virulenceFactor: Induction of vascular endothelial proliferation producing angioproliferative lesions, and intracellular persistence in erythrocytes and endothelium
organisms.tooltip: In immunocompetent hosts it causes self-limited regional adenopathy; in HIV it drives vascular proliferation (bacillary angiomatosis), which can be mistaken for Kaposi sarcoma.

organisms.name: Treponema pallidum
organisms.labFeatures: Thin spirochete not visible on Gram stain and not culturable; dark-field microscopy, VDRL and RPR screening, FTA-ABS confirmation
organisms.manifestations: Primary painless chancre; secondary diffuse maculopapular rash including palms and soles, condyloma lata; tertiary gummas, tabes dorsalis, Argyll Robertson pupils, aortitis; congenital syphilis with snuffles and saber shins
organisms.treatment: Penicillin G at every stage, with dose and duration by stage; desensitize penicillin-allergic pregnant patients rather than substitute
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact with a moist lesion; transplacental transmission causing congenital syphilis
organisms.virulenceFactor: Outer membrane with very few surface proteins to limit antibody recognition, plus antigenic variation allowing immune evasion
organisms.tooltip: Primary chancre is painless, unlike chancroid from H. ducreyi. Treatment can precipitate the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — fever and myalgias hours after penicillin from lysed organisms.

organisms.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
organisms.labFeatures: Large spirochete visible on Giemsa stain; serologic ELISA with Western blot confirmation; clinical diagnosis when erythema migrans is present
organisms.manifestations: Stage 1 erythema migrans target rash with flu-like illness; stage 2 facial nerve palsy, AV block, migratory arthralgia; stage 3 chronic monoarticular arthritis and encephalopathy
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline for early disease; amoxicillin or cefuroxime in children and pregnancy; ceftriaxone for carditis or neurologic involvement
organisms.transmission: Bite of the Ixodes scapularis tick, with the white-footed mouse as reservoir and deer as the adult tick host; requires 24 to 48 hours of attachment
organisms.virulenceFactor: Outer surface protein antigenic variation (VlsE) for immune evasion, and the ability to disseminate widely through tissue
organisms.tooltip: The Ixodes tick also transmits Babesia and Anaplasma, so coinfection is common. Bell palsy plus a target rash plus heart block in a Northeast hiker is the classic picture.

organisms.name: Leptospira interrogans
organisms.labFeatures: Thin spirochete with hooked ends on dark-field microscopy, grows in Fletcher medium, serology or PCR; conjunctival suffusion without discharge
organisms.manifestations: Flu-like illness with severe myalgias, conjunctival suffusion, and photophobia; Weil disease with jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage
organisms.treatment: Penicillin G or doxycycline; doxycycline for prophylaxis in high-risk exposure
organisms.transmission: Contact with water contaminated by animal urine, especially dog and rodent; surfers and tropical travelers, and flooding events
organisms.virulenceFactor: Motility and tissue invasiveness allowing penetration of intact mucosa and skin, with vascular endothelial damage
organisms.tooltip: Conjunctival suffusion — red eyes without discharge — plus severe calf myalgias in a surfer or someone exposed to floodwater. Weil disease is the severe icteric form with renal failure.

organisms.name: Chlamydia trachomatis
organisms.labFeatures: Obligate intracellular organism lacking muramic acid in its peptidoglycan; cytoplasmic inclusions on Giemsa; nucleic acid amplification testing for diagnosis
organisms.manifestations: Nongonococcal urethritis and cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, reactive arthritis, lymphogranuloma venereum, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia, and trachoma causing blindness
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin or doxycycline; erythromycin for neonates; azithromycin for mass treatment of trachoma
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact; vertical transmission at delivery; eye-seeking flies and fingers for trachoma serotypes A through C
organisms.virulenceFactor: Two-form life cycle — the infectious extracellular elementary body and the replicative intracellular reticulate body — plus inhibition of phagolysosome fusion
organisms.tooltip: It cannot make its own ATP, so it is an energy parasite. Serotypes A to C cause trachoma, D to K cause genital and neonatal disease, and L1 to L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum.

organisms.name: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
organisms.labFeatures: No cell wall, so invisible on Gram stain and unaffected by beta-lactams; membrane contains cholesterol; fried-egg colonies on Eaton agar; positive cold agglutinins
organisms.manifestations: Walking pneumonia in young adults with persistent dry cough and chest x-ray findings worse than the exam suggests; bullous myringitis; erythema multiforme; cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin, doxycycline, or a fluoroquinolone; beta-lactams are useless
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets in close quarters — military recruits, college dormitories, and prisons
organisms.virulenceFactor: P1 adhesin binds respiratory epithelium; hydrogen peroxide production damages cilia; no endotoxin since there is no cell wall
organisms.tooltip: No cell wall means no Gram stain and no beta-lactam susceptibility. The only bacterium with cholesterol in its membrane. Cold agglutinin IgM can cause hemolysis — a favorite exam link.

organisms.name: Rickettsia rickettsii
organisms.labFeatures: Obligate intracellular gram-negative organism, Giemsa stain, serology for diagnosis; Weil-Felix historically positive; thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia common
organisms.manifestations: Rocky Mountain spotted fever — fever, severe headache, then a rash starting on wrists and ankles that spreads centrally and involves palms and soles; vasculitis and shock
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline started empirically on clinical suspicion, including in children, since delay is fatal
organisms.transmission: Dermacentor tick bite, most commonly in the south Atlantic and south central United States despite the name
organisms.virulenceFactor: Replication within vascular endothelium causing widespread small-vessel vasculitis, increased permeability, and consumptive thrombocytopenia
organisms.tooltip: Rash starts peripherally and moves inward — the reverse of typhus, which starts centrally and spares palms and soles. Treat on suspicion; waiting for serology costs lives.

organisms.name: Coxiella burnetii
organisms.labFeatures: Obligate intracellular organism with a spore-like stable form, no arthropod vector required, serology for diagnosis; the exception to most Rickettsial rules
organisms.manifestations: Q fever with pneumonia, high fever, and hepatitis with granulomas; chronic Q fever causing culture-negative endocarditis
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline; add hydroxychloroquine for chronic Q fever endocarditis, often for 18 months or more
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of aerosols from infected cattle, sheep, and goat placenta, hides, or amniotic fluid; no tick bite needed
organisms.virulenceFactor: Resistant spore-like form surviving environmental drying, plus replication inside the acidified phagolysosome of macrophages
organisms.tooltip: The Rickettsial exception: no rash, no vector, spore-forming, and spread by aerosol. Think farm animals and parturition. A classic cause of culture-negative endocarditis.

organisms.name: Anaplasma phagocytophilum
organisms.labFeatures: Obligate intracellular organism forming morulae within granulocytes on peripheral smear; leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases; PCR confirms
organisms.manifestations: Human granulocytic anaplasmosis with fever, headache, and myalgias, typically without a rash
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline
organisms.transmission: Ixodes tick bite, the same vector as Lyme disease and Babesia, so coinfection is common
organisms.virulenceFactor: Replication within neutrophil vacuoles while inhibiting the respiratory burst and delaying apoptosis of the host cell
organisms.tooltip: Fever and headache with cytopenias and no rash after a tick bite. Morulae inside granulocytes are the key smear finding; Ehrlichia forms them inside monocytes instead.

organisms.name: Gardnerella vaginalis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-variable pleomorphic rod; clue cells (epithelial cells coated with bacteria) on wet mount, vaginal pH above 4.5, positive whiff test with potassium hydroxide
organisms.manifestations: Bacterial vaginosis with thin gray-white malodorous discharge and minimal inflammation; associated with preterm labor
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole or clindamycin, oral or intravaginal
organisms.transmission: Overgrowth of endogenous flora with loss of protective lactobacilli, associated with douching and new sexual partners
organisms.virulenceFactor: Biofilm formation on vaginal epithelium and production of amines (the fishy odor) as lactobacilli are displaced
organisms.tooltip: Vaginosis, not vaginitis — there is little inflammation, which is why there is no itching or dysuria. Clue cells plus a positive whiff test plus pH above 4.5 clinches it.

organisms.name: Bacteroides fragilis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative obligate anaerobic rod, bile resistant, grows below the diaphragm, lacks lipid A potency so endotoxin is weak
organisms.manifestations: Intra-abdominal abscess after bowel perforation, peritonitis, pelvic abscess, and polymicrobial surgical site infection
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem; drainage of abscesses
organisms.transmission: Endogenous colonic flora spilling into the peritoneum after perforation, surgery, or diverticulitis
organisms.virulenceFactor: Polysaccharide capsule promoting abscess formation, superoxide dismutase and catalase for brief oxygen tolerance, and beta-lactamase production
organisms.tooltip: The dominant anaerobe below the diaphragm; above the diaphragm think Peptostreptococcus and oral anaerobes. Its capsule is what drives abscess formation.

organisms.name: Haemophilus ducreyi
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative coccobacillus in a school-of-fish arrangement, fastidious requiring enriched chocolate agar, usually a clinical diagnosis
organisms.manifestations: Chancroid — one or more deep painful genital ulcers with ragged undermined edges and tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin single dose, or ceftriaxone
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact, most common in tropical and subtropical regions
organisms.virulenceFactor: Cytolethal distending toxin causing tissue necrosis and ulceration, and resistance to serum killing
organisms.tooltip: 'Do cry' — H. ducreyi ulcers are painful, unlike the painless syphilitic chancre. Painful ulcer plus tender suppurative nodes is the distinguishing pair.

organisms.name: Klebsiella granulomatis
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod seen as intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies in macrophages on Giemsa stain; difficult to culture
organisms.manifestations: Granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) — a painless beefy-red ulcer that bleeds readily, without lymphadenopathy
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline or azithromycin for at least three weeks until lesions heal
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact, endemic in tropical regions including India, Papua New Guinea, and parts of Africa
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intracellular survival in macrophages producing chronic granulomatous ulceration with vascular friable tissue
organisms.tooltip: Donovan bodies in macrophages. A beefy-red painless ulcer that bleeds easily and notably lacks lymphadenopathy — which distinguishes it from chancroid and lymphogranuloma venereum.

organisms.name: Ureaplasma urealyticum
organisms.labFeatures: No cell wall, urease positive, requires urea for growth, not seen on Gram stain, PCR for diagnosis
organisms.manifestations: Nongonococcal urethritis, especially persistent cases after chlamydia has been treated; chorioamnionitis and neonatal pneumonia
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline or azithromycin; beta-lactams are ineffective
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact; vertical transmission to the neonate
organisms.virulenceFactor: Urease generating ammonia that damages urothelium, plus adherence to mucosal epithelium
organisms.tooltip: Consider it in persistent urethritis after treating gonorrhea and chlamydia. Like Mycoplasma it has no cell wall, so beta-lactams do nothing — and urease positivity distinguishes it.

organisms.name: Mycobacterium avium complex
organisms.labFeatures: Acid-fast bacilli, slow growing, environmental nontuberculous mycobacteria; blood culture positive in disseminated disease with CD4 below 50
organisms.manifestations: Disseminated infection with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and anemia in advanced HIV; cavitary lung disease in COPD; Lady Windermere syndrome; cervical lymphadenitis in children
organisms.treatment: Azithromycin plus ethambutol plus rifabutin; azithromycin prophylaxis when CD4 is below 50
organisms.transmission: Environmental exposure to water and soil aerosols; no person-to-person transmission
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intracellular survival in macrophages with resistance to lysosomal killing; intrinsic multidrug resistance from the lipid-rich cell wall
organisms.tooltip: A CD4 count below 50 is the threshold for both disease and prophylaxis. Lady Windermere syndrome is right middle lobe disease in thin elderly women who habitually suppress cough.

organisms.name: Burkholderia cepacia complex
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, oxidase positive, lactose non-fermenter, aerobe, highly antibiotic resistant, grows on selective OFPBL agar
organisms.manifestations: Rapidly progressive pneumonia and cepacia syndrome in cystic fibrosis; infection in chronic granulomatous disease; nosocomial outbreaks from contaminated solutions
organisms.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, meropenem, or ceftazidime guided by susceptibilities; often multidrug resistant
organisms.transmission: Person-to-person among cystic fibrosis patients (hence segregation policies), and contaminated medical solutions and disinfectants
organisms.virulenceFactor: Extreme intrinsic antibiotic resistance, biofilm formation, and cable pili mediating adherence to respiratory epithelium
organisms.tooltip: A feared cystic fibrosis pathogen because it can cause fulminant decline and is a contraindication to lung transplant at many centers. CF patients are kept apart to prevent its spread.

organisms.name: Serratia marcescens
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose non-fermenter (slow), red prodigiosin pigment, DNase positive, motile, AmpC beta-lactamase producer
organisms.manifestations: Nosocomial urinary tract and respiratory infection, catheter-related bloodstream infection, endocarditis in injection drug users
organisms.treatment: Carbapenem or cefepime; avoid third-generation cephalosporins because AmpC induction causes resistance during therapy
organisms.transmission: Contaminated hospital equipment, catheters, intravenous fluids, and hands of healthcare workers
organisms.virulenceFactor: AmpC beta-lactamase inducible during treatment, biofilm formation on catheters, and extracellular DNase and proteases
organisms.tooltip: Red pigment is the memorable clue. It belongs to the SPACE organisms (Serratia, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter) that induce AmpC and defeat cephalosporins mid-course.

organisms.name: Acinetobacter baumannii
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative coccobacillus, oxidase negative, non-motile, strict aerobe, lactose non-fermenter, survives on dry surfaces for weeks
organisms.manifestations: Ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infection, wound infection in combat casualties, and meningitis after neurosurgery
organisms.treatment: Carbapenem if susceptible; colistin, tigecycline, or cefiderocol for carbapenem-resistant strains
organisms.transmission: Contaminated ICU surfaces, ventilator circuits, and healthcare worker hands; notorious in combat trauma
organisms.virulenceFactor: Extraordinary environmental persistence, efflux pumps and carbapenemases, and biofilm formation on plastic
organisms.tooltip: Among the most antibiotic-resistant organisms in medicine and remarkably hardy on dry surfaces, which is why ICU outbreaks are so hard to clear. Oxidase negative, unlike Pseudomonas.

organisms.name: Enterobacter species
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative rod, lactose fermenter, motile, oxidase negative, inducible AmpC beta-lactamase
organisms.manifestations: Nosocomial pneumonia, urinary tract infection, surgical site infection, and bacteremia
organisms.treatment: Cefepime or a carbapenem; third-generation cephalosporins fail because AmpC is derepressed during treatment
organisms.transmission: Nosocomial spread from hospital flora, devices, and healthcare worker hands
organisms.virulenceFactor: Inducible AmpC beta-lactamase causing treatment-emergent resistance, plus endotoxin and biofilm formation
organisms.tooltip: The classic AmpC trap: the isolate tests susceptible to ceftriaxone, the patient improves, then relapses with a now-resistant organism. Use cefepime or a carbapenem from the start.

organisms.name: Pasteurella multocida
organisms.labFeatures: Gram-negative coccobacillus with bipolar staining, oxidase positive, catalase positive, grows on blood agar but not MacConkey
organisms.manifestations: Rapidly progressive cellulitis within 24 hours of a cat or dog bite, with lymphangitis; osteomyelitis and septic arthritis if deeper structures are involved
organisms.treatment: Amoxicillin-clavulanate; doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone plus clindamycin if penicillin allergic
organisms.transmission: Cat and dog bites and scratches; cat bites are higher risk because they inoculate deeply
organisms.virulenceFactor: Polysaccharide capsule resisting phagocytosis, plus endotoxin and dermonecrotic toxin
organisms.tooltip: Cellulitis appearing within a day of an animal bite points here; staph and strep cellulitis take longer. Amoxicillin-clavulanate covers it plus the oral anaerobes also inoculated by the bite.
